Bankruptcy is a legal status — officially recognized by a court of law — in which a person or organization is formally declared unable to repay the money they owe to others. It is not about being temporarily tight on cash. It means the financial situation has become so overwhelmed by debt that repaying what is owed is genuinely impossible, even in the foreseeable future. When this point is reached, the person or organization can go to a court and formally declare: "I cannot pay my debts." This triggers a structured legal process that decides what happens next, fairly and in an orderly way.
The Key People Involved

Three roles are central to every bankruptcy case. The debtor is the person or organization that owes money and has entered the bankruptcy process. The creditor is anyone the debtor owes money to — a bank, a credit card company, a landlord, a supplier, or even a private individual. The trustee is a court-appointed official who manages the case, examines the debtor's financial situation, ensures the process is fair, and distributes any available money to creditors.
What Actually Happens When Someone Files

The moment someone files for bankruptcy, the court immediately issues what is called an automatic stay. This is a legal freeze that instantly stops all creditors from taking any collection actions — no more demand letters, no phone calls, no lawsuits, no repossessions — at least while the case is being resolved. This gives the debtor some breathing room to participate in the process without being hounded.

From there, what happens depends on which type of bankruptcy is filed.
Insolvency vs. Bankruptcy — An Important Distinction

These two words are often confused, so it is worth separating them clearly. Insolvency is the financial condition of being unable to pay your debts — it is purely about your financial state and can exist quietly, without anyone else knowing. Bankruptcy, on the other hand, is the formal legal process that follows when an insolvent person or organization goes to court to have that condition officially recognized and dealt with. In short: insolvency is the problem; bankruptcy is the legal response to that problem.
Voluntary vs. Involuntary Bankruptcy

Bankruptcy can be initiated in two ways. Voluntary bankruptcy is by far the most common — the debtor themselves chooses to file, deciding that the legal process is the best way to deal with an impossible debt situation. Involuntary bankruptcy, on the other hand, is when creditors petition the court to force a debtor into bankruptcy because the debtor owes them money and refuses to pay or has become clearly unable to. Courts are generally careful about granting involuntary petitions and require creditors to meet strict conditions before doing so.
The Main Types of Bankruptcy

In the United States — which has one of the most developed bankruptcy systems in the world — the types of bankruptcy are referred to by chapter numbers from the federal law. The most common are Chapter 7, Chapter 11, and Chapter 13. Other countries have their own equivalent systems with different names, but the core ideas are broadly similar worldwide.

Chapter 7 is known as liquidation bankruptcy. A trustee is appointed to sell off the debtor's non-exempt assets (more on exemptions shortly), and the money raised is distributed among creditors. Most remaining eligible debts are then discharged — meaning legally wiped away. The debtor loses many possessions but gets a clean financial slate. This is commonly used by individuals with little income and substantial unsecured debt, such as credit card balances or medical bills.

Chapter 11 is known as reorganization bankruptcy and is primarily used by businesses. Rather than shutting down entirely, the business proposes a plan to restructure its debts — negotiating lower payments, extended timelines, or reduced amounts owed — while continuing to operate. Airlines, large retailers, and major corporations have used Chapter 11 when they were in serious financial trouble but believed the business could survive with restructuring.

Chapter 13 is a repayment plan designed for individuals who have a regular income. Instead of liquidating assets, the debtor proposes a plan to repay all or part of their debts over three to five years, often at reduced amounts. This is especially useful for people who want to keep their home or car while catching up on overdue payments.
What Gets Discharged — and What Doesn't

When a debt is discharged, the debtor is no longer legally obligated to pay it, and creditors can never legally come after them for it again. This is the "fresh start" that bankruptcy promises. However, not all debts can be discharged, and this is one of the most critical things to understand.

Debts that typically cannot be wiped away include student loans (in most circumstances in the US), child support and alimony, most tax debts owed to the government, debts arising from fraud or deliberate wrongdoing, and criminal fines or penalties. These survive bankruptcy completely intact — the debtor must still pay them in full, no matter what.
Exempt Assets — What You Get to Keep

Bankruptcy does not mean losing absolutely everything you own. Exemptions are legal protections that shield certain categories of assets from being seized and sold to pay creditors. The exact exemptions vary by country and, in the US, by state — but they commonly include a portion of the value of your primary home (called a homestead exemption), a vehicle up to a certain value, basic household goods and clothing, tools you need to do your job, and certain retirement accounts. The underlying idea is that the legal system does not want to leave debtors completely destitute with nothing to rebuild from.
The Consequences of Bankruptcy

Filing for bankruptcy has real and lasting consequences beyond the courtroom.

The most significant is the damage to your credit score — the numerical rating that tells lenders how trustworthy you are as a borrower. A Chapter 7 bankruptcy stays on your credit report for ten years, while a Chapter 13 typically stays for seven. During this period, getting approved for loans, mortgages, credit cards, or even rental apartments becomes very difficult, as lenders view you as a high-risk borrower. Interest rates, if you do get approved for credit, will often be much higher than normal.

Bankruptcy is also a public record, meaning it can be looked up by employers, landlords, or anyone who searches for it. This can affect your ability to get jobs that involve financial responsibility, or to rent a home from a landlord who checks backgrounds.

There can also be social stigma attached to bankruptcy, as some people associate it with personal failure or irresponsibility — though this perception is often unfair, since many bankruptcies are caused by circumstances beyond a person's control, such as sudden medical emergencies, job loss, or economic collapse.

That said, bankruptcy is very deliberately designed to allow for recovery. Many individuals and businesses have successfully rebuilt their finances and reputations after going through the process.
Bankruptcy for Businesses vs. Individuals

While individuals typically file for bankruptcy after personal financial disasters — job loss, divorce, overwhelming medical bills, or unmanageable debt — businesses file when they can no longer meet their financial obligations to suppliers, lenders, employees, or bondholders.

When a business liquidates through bankruptcy, there is a strict legal priority order for who gets paid first. Secured creditors — those whose loans are backed by collateral, such as a bank that holds a mortgage on a building — are paid before unsecured creditors, such as suppliers or credit card companies. Shareholders are usually last in line and often receive nothing. This priority order ensures the process is predictable and fair, even if no one gets everything they are owed.
The Figurative Meaning

Beyond its strict legal definition, "bankruptcy" is widely used in everyday language to describe a complete and total absence of something valuable — not just money. You will regularly hear expressions like moral bankruptcy, which describes a person, institution, or government that has completely abandoned ethical principles and has no integrity left. Similarly, intellectual bankruptcy describes arguments, ideas, or positions that are so devoid of substance or logic that they have nothing real to offer.

In this figurative sense, the word carries its core meaning — total emptiness, utter failure, an inability to produce anything of worth — and simply applies it beyond the financial world.
Real-World Examples

To make this concrete: imagine a person who loses their job, accumulates enormous medical bills after a serious illness, and falls deeply behind on credit card payments. Their income, even after recovery, will never realistically be enough to repay the full debt. They file for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. The court discharges the eligible debts, they surrender non-exempt assets, their credit takes a hit, but they are legally free of those obligations and can start rebuilding.

On the business side, both United Airlines and Delta Air Lines filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the early 2000s. Rather than shutting down, they restructured their debts, renegotiated contracts with employees and suppliers, and continued operating. Both eventually emerged from bankruptcy and went on to become financially healthy airlines again. This illustrates something important: bankruptcy, especially for businesses, does not always mean permanent failure. It can be a painful but survivable reset.
The Single-Sentence Summary

If you had to reduce "bankruptcy" to its essence: it is the formal legal process by which a court officially recognizes that a person or organization cannot repay their debts, and then oversees a fair resolution — either by wiping those debts away, reorganizing them, or creating a repayment plan — so that both the debtor and the creditors are treated as justly as the circumstances allow.
